name: Tetrapeptide-21

card.summary: A four-amino-acid (GEKG) matrix-supporting cosmetic peptide; research so far is on skin delivery and cell-culture effects, not human trials.
card.note: No published human efficacy trial in the available literature.

quick.overview:
Tetrapeptide-21 is a short cosmetic peptide with the amino acid sequence GEKG, sold in anti-aging serums as a matrix-supporting ingredient. Papers describe it as having collagen-stimulating, anti-aging activity.

Most published work concerns how to get it through the skin, with a 2018 delivery study and a 2026 hydrogel study, plus an in vitro fibroblast study. No human clinical trial of its appearance effects was found.
quick.mechanism: It is described as stimulating collagen and the extracellular matrix [2]. Because peptides are large, polar and easily degraded, researchers have studied enhancer molecules, carrier systems and elastin-derived hydrogels to improve skin delivery [1][2].
quick.risks: No safety data from human trials were found. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not an approved drug.

lead: Tetrapeptide-21 is a four-amino-acid cosmetic peptide (sequence GEKG) used in anti-aging skincare to help skin look firmer and smoother by supporting the collagen-rich matrix beneath the surface. It is applied topically in serums and creams. Published papers describe it as demonstrating anti-aging efficacy and stimulating collagen [2].

It belongs to the family of cosmetic signal peptides alongside palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl), a matrikine launched by Sederma in 2000 and described as boosting synthesis of extracellular matrix molecules [4]. Laboratory work has studied GEKG together with Matrixyl in cultured skin cells [3].

The literature on it is mostly formulation science: peptides are hard to deliver into skin because of their size, hydrophilicity, polarity and susceptibility to enzymatic degradation [1]. No human clinical trial of its effect on appearance was found.

paras: A 2018 study in the European Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences examined enhancer molecules and colloidal carrier systems to improve dermal bioavailability of GEKG, noting that peptide delivery into skin is challenging [1]. A 2026 study in the International Journal of Pharmaceutics designed elastin-derived peptide hydrogels for sustained dermal delivery of tetrapeptide-21 [2]. In the 2018 work, ex vivo experiments on human skin at three incubation times compared a nano-sized microemulsion and enhancers with a standard formulation to see how deeply and in which layers GEKG penetrated [1]. In the 2026 hydrogel study, the hydrogels sustained permeation at 7.5 to 20.9 percent over 72 hours versus 26.6 percent for the free peptide solution, giving slower, controlled release [2].

Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Pal-KTTKS) is described on Wikipedia as a messenger peptide whose attached fatty chain helps it cross skin lipids, with studies cited including a 2005 report on topical use in photoaged facial skin [4]. Tetrapeptide-21 is marketed in the same category of matrix-supporting ingredients, though Wikipedia's Matrixyl article does not discuss it [4].

A 2025 in vitro study in Molecules examined injectable platelet-rich fibrin together with cosmetic peptides, including Matrixyl, on dermal fibroblast viability and extracellular matrix gene expression [3]. These are cell-culture findings and do not show effects on living human skin. In that study the combination of injectable platelet-rich fibrin with GEKG increased cell viability and upregulated the matrix-related genes COL1A1, FN1 and HAS1 at 72 hours, and more strongly than either treatment alone [3].
No studies found. Related laboratory research on delivery systems and cultured fibroblasts exists [1][2][3].

Described as stimulating collagen and extracellular matrix in skin cells
Skin aims to look firmer and smoother over time
angle.text: People use peptide serums containing tetrapeptide-21 hoping for firmer, smoother-looking skin and fewer visible signs of aging. The proposed route is through support of collagen and the extracellular matrix.
